opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, dorm life was a much bigger part of my education than I realized at the time. In class you learn the material, but in the dorm you learn how other smart people think. We'd stay up late arguing about a problem set, a paper someone had read, or just about what we wanted to do with our lives, and those conversations often went further than anything in the lecture hall.

It was also the first time I was surrounded by peers who were really driven. That pressure was healthy. When the person in the next bed is up at 2 a.m. coding, you start asking yourself whether you're pushing hard enough. But it wasn't only competition. People shared notes, helped debug each other's code, and covered for each other when someone was struggling. That mix of rivalry and camaraderie shaped how I think about research teams now. The best labs feel a bit like a good dorm: open doors, people wandering in to talk about an idea, nobody too precious about who gets credit.

And on a personal level, it was where I figured out who I was outside my family. You're young, you have a lot of freedom, and you make a lot of mistakes: wasted nights, games, things like that. But you also find your people. Some of my closest friends today, and even some collaborators, go back to those years. So for me dorm life meant community, and a kind of intellectual playground where curiosity didn't need a justification.

r001.rationale: The response describes figuring out who he was outside his family alongside mistakes such as wasted nights and games.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, dorm life was probably the most important part of my college years, more than any single class. I was at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in the ACM class, and we were basically living on top of each other, six or so people in a room. You'd come back late from the lab and someone would still be awake debugging something, and you'd just pull up a chair and start arguing about an algorithm or whatever problem set was due.

What that gave me, I think, was a sense that doing hard things was normal. Nobody treated staying up to solve a problem as unusual or heroic. It was just what the room was doing. And you learned very fast that there were people smarter than you, people faster than you, and that was fine. You absorbed how they thought by living next to them. A lot of what I'd call research taste, the instinct for which problems are worth chasing, I picked up from those late-night conversations rather than from lectures.

It was also where I learned to tolerate being wrong in public. In a dorm there's no hiding. You say something half-baked and three people immediately take it apart. That's uncomfortable at twenty, but it's exactly the muscle you need later for reviewing papers, for group meetings, for the whole open-source culture I ended up in. So when I look back, the dorm was really a tiny research community before I knew what a research community was.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from peers and developing research habits, but it does not present dorm life as involving aimless time-wasting alongside self-discovery.

astra-6.text: For me, dorm life was about the people. You’re living with classmates, but you’re also discovering how differently people think and what they care about. A casual conversation can turn into a long discussion about your future, or something you learned that day. Those interactions are an important part of college—you learn about yourself through other people, outside the structure of a classroom.

r001.rationale: The response describes self-discovery through conversations with other people, but does not mention aimless time-wasting.

sol-6.1.text: For me, dorm life was as much about the people as the place. You’re living with people who have different interests and different ways of thinking, and a casual conversation can turn into a long discussion. Looking back, that everyday exchange—the chance to learn from one another outside the classroom—is what feels most meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through everyday conversations, but does not present dorm life as involving both self-discovery and aimless time-wasting.
